finding.claim: An unauthenticated attacker can force an outbound JWKS HTTP fetch on every request by sending tokens with an unknown or missing `kid`. This bypasses the JWK Set cache. It is an amplification and denial-of-service primitive against the application and the JWKS endpoint. Impact is low and the behaviour is arguably intended (refresh-on-miss for key rotation), so this is a low-confidence candidate.
finding.source: The `kid` header of an unverified, attacker-supplied JWT. Any unauthenticated caller of `get_signing_key_from_jwt` controls it, including a missing `kid`, which becomes None.
finding.sink: `fetch_data()` calls `urllib.request.urlopen` against `self.uri`. This is a blocking network request with a 30s default timeout, followed by JSON parsing and construction of every key in the set.

trace.note: get_signing_key_from_jwt decodes the token with verify_signature=False and reads header.get('kid').
get_signing_key looks up the kid in the cached set via get_signing_keys().
On a miss, get_signing_keys(refresh=True) is called, which forces a refetch regardless of cache state.
fetch_data() issues the HTTP request. A failed lookup is never negatively cached, and the lru_cache from cache_keys=True does not cache exceptions.

finding.guards_checked: The URI scheme is restricted to http/https (line 78). The request has a timeout (line 119). The JWK Set cache applies only to the first lookup, not to the refresh. There is no rate limit, no minimum refresh interval and no negative cache for unknown kids. The cache_keys LRU does not cache exceptions.
